title: The Lesson I Learned From Paul’s Thorn
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Paul’s Thorn
The Pain God Would Not Remove Became the Grace That Changed Everything
There are prayers we celebrate because God answered them.
Then there are prayers we rarely talk about.
The ones that seemed to disappear into silence.
The ones whispered through tears at midnight.
The ones repeated so many times that eventually your voice becomes tired.
The ones that leave you wondering whether heaven heard you at all.
I know those prayers.
Maybe you do too.
Maybe yours sounds like the prayer of a mother watching her child walk away from God.
Maybe yours is the prayer of a husband trying to save a marriage.
Maybe yours is the prayer of someone carrying anxiety, depression, grief, loneliness, betrayal, addiction, regret, or a wound that never seems to heal.
You prayed.
You fasted.
You believed.
You waited.
And somehow the thorn remained.
That is why the story of Paul’s thorn is one of the most personal and powerful passages in all of Scripture.
Because it speaks directly to every believer who has ever asked God, “Why haven’t You taken this away?”
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 12:7:
The Greek phrase Paul uses is σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (skolops tē sarki).
A skolops was not a tiny inconvenience.
It referred to a sharp stake, splinter, or painful object that pierced deeply.
Paul is describing something that hurt.
Something persistent.
Something he could not ignore.
Something that followed him.
For centuries believers have debated what the thorn was.
Poor eyesight.
A physical illness.
Persecution.
Spiritual attacks.
Some recurring affliction.
The truth is that God never tells us exactly what it was.
Perhaps because if God had named Paul's thorn, we might dismiss it as different from our own.
Instead, God leaves it unnamed so every wounded believer can see themselves in the story.
Paul continues:
“For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.” (2 Corinthians 12:8)
Three times.
Not once.
Not casually.
Not half-heartedly.
The apostle who raised the dead.
The apostle who planted churches.
The apostle who saw visions of heaven.
The apostle who wrote much of the New Testament.
Even he begged God to remove his thorn.
And God said no.
That truth shocks many Christians.
Because somewhere along the way we began believing that strong faith always produces immediate relief.
Yet Scripture repeatedly shows something different.
Sometimes God calms the storm.
Sometimes He calms His child while the storm continues.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking statements ever spoken by God.
2 Corinthians 12:9:
“And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
The Greek reads:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου (Arkei soi hē charis mou)
Literally:
“My grace is enough for you.”
Enough.
Not almost enough.
Not barely enough.
Enough.
The word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, kindness, and divine empowerment.
God was not merely offering sympathy.
He was offering Himself.
Paul asked for removal.
God offered presence.
Paul asked for freedom from pain.
God offered strength inside pain.
Paul asked for deliverance.
God offered grace.
And grace proved greater.
The lesson that changed my life came when I finally realized that God often does His deepest work through the very thing I am begging Him to remove.
We naturally assume our greatest obstacle is the thing standing in our way.
God often sees it as the tool shaping us into Christ.
Without the thorn, Paul might have trusted his revelations.
With the thorn, he learned dependence.
Without the thorn, Paul might have gloried in his accomplishments.
With the thorn, he gloried in God's strength.
Without the thorn, Paul might have become self-sufficient.
With the thorn, he became Christ-dependent.
How many of us have prayed for God to remove the very thing He is using to transform us?
That question hurts.
Because it forces us to confront something we do not like.
God's primary goal is not our comfort.
His primary goal is our conformity to Christ.
Romans 8:29 declares that believers are predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son.
The Father is far more committed to our holiness than our convenience.
Far more committed to eternal transformation than temporary relief.
That is difficult theology until life breaks your heart.
Then it becomes survival.
There are seasons when God heals instantly.
Praise Him.
There are seasons when God opens doors miraculously.
Praise Him.
There are seasons when God removes mountains.
Praise Him.
But there are also seasons when the mountain remains.
The thorn remains.
The struggle remains.
And in those moments God whispers the same words He spoke to Paul:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Not because He has abandoned you.
Because He is carrying you.
Not because He is distant.
Because He is closer than you realize.
Not because He does not care.
Because His plans are larger than your pain.
One of the most beautiful truths hidden inside this passage is that Paul's greatest weakness became one of his greatest testimonies.
The thing he wanted removed became part of the story God used to strengthen millions of believers across generations.
Even today, nearly two thousand years later, wounded Christians find comfort in a struggle that Paul wished had ended.
Imagine that.
The pain he wanted erased became part of his legacy.
The wound became a witness.
The weakness became a testimony.
The thorn became a sermon.
And perhaps the same is true for you.
Maybe one day someone will survive because you stayed faithful.
Maybe someone will believe because you endured.
Maybe someone will find hope because they watched God sustain you when everything seemed impossible.
The Hebrew Scriptures often use the word חֶסֶד (chesed) to describe God's covenant love.
There is no perfect English equivalent.
It means steadfast love.
Faithful mercy.
Lovingkindness that refuses to let go.
When your thorn remains, His chesed remains.
When your strength fails, His chesed remains.
When your answers never arrive, His chesed remains.
When your tears fall unseen, His chesed remains.
The enemy wants you to believe your thorn proves God has forgotten you.
The Gospel declares the opposite.
The cross forever settled God's love.
Jesus Christ entered suffering Himself.
He was betrayed.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And through what appeared to be the greatest scandal in history, God brought the greatest act of grace the world has ever known.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
It is biblical reality.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became victory.
The tomb looked final.
It became the beginning.
Peter looked disqualified.
He became restored.
Paul looked broken.
He became powerful through weakness.
And perhaps your story is not ending where you think it is.
Perhaps God is still writing.
Perhaps the thorn is not proof that your life is ruined.
Perhaps it is evidence that the Author has not finished the chapter.
If this article spoke to your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
What thorn has God used to draw you closer to Him?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
If you desire to glorify God through advancing biblical content that reaches the lost, strengthens believers, and spreads the Gospel to more people every day, your support truly makes a difference.
Because one shared article can reach a wounded heart.
One testimony can strengthen a struggling believer.
One act of support can help spread the Gospel farther than you may ever know.
And sometimes the thorn you wish God would remove becomes the very place where His grace shines brightest.
The thorn never had the final word. Grace did.
